answers.answer: No. SCOPe does not support merging them into one homologous superfamily. In the current release, SCOPe 2.08 (freeze 2021-07-28, release 2021-09-22, latest periodic update 2.08-2026-08-16), all three groups sit in class f (membrane and cell surface proteins and peptides) under a single fold, f.21 'Heme-binding four-helical bundle' (sunid 81344), but as three distinct superfamilies: f.21.1 'Transmembrane di-heme cytochromes' (sunid 81342; families include f.21.1.1, the E. coli formate dehydrogenase cytochrome b subunit, and f.21.1.2, cytochrome b6 of the b6f complex, e.g. d1vf5a_/d1vf5n_ from 1vf5), f.21.2 'Fumarate reductase respiratory complex transmembrane subunits' (sunid 81343; family f.21.2.1 with Wolinella succinogenes FrdC and the E. coli SdhC/SdhD-type subunits), and f.21.3 'Respiratory nitrate reductase 1 gamma chain' (sunid 103501; family f.21.3.1, E. coli NarI). In SCOP/SCOPe the fold level records only a shared major secondary-structure arrangement and topology (here, a four-transmembrane-helix bundle with two b-type hemes ligated between helix pairs); it does not assert common ancestry. The superfamily level is the evolutionary unit, and the curators deliberately kept these three apart because sequence similarity is undetectable and the shared architecture plus heme chemistry can be explained by convergence or by generic constraints on bis-His heme ligation in a helical bundle. So the correct statement is: same fold (f.21), same class (f), but three separate superfamilies with no homology claimed. Limits: (1) fold-level co-membership must not be used to transfer function, cofactor stoichiometry, or quinone-site details between these groups; e.g. the di-heme formate dehydrogenase cytochrome b, the fumarate reductase/succinate dehydrogenase membrane anchors (which vary from one-heme to two-heme), and NarI differ in heme number, ligation details, and electron-transfer partners. (2) Homology-based template modelling across superfamilies is unsafe; a template should be chosen from the same family or superfamily, and cross-superfamily use should be treated as fold-level analogy only. (3) Evidence that would be required to justify a merge is not provided by SCOPe: statistically significant sequence or profile-HMM similarity (e.g. HHpred/Pfam clan evidence), conserved sequence motifs around the heme-ligating histidines beyond what the architecture dictates, conserved genomic/operon context, or superposition-based structural similarity exceeding what unrelated four-helix bundles achieve. Note also that SCOPe 2.08 adds new entries to existing families largely by automated assignment and did not re-curate these superfamilies, so the fold/superfamily split reflects the manually curated SCOP 1.75 judgment carried forward. If a user needs a single evolutionary grouping across all three, SCOPe is the wrong source; they should cite the fold f.21 as a structural (not homologous) grouping and look to ECOD or Pfam-clan evidence for any claim of distant homology.
